'''Eintracht Frankfurt e.V.''' ({{IPA|de|ˈaɪntʁaxt ˈfʁaŋkfʊʁt|-|De-Eintracht Frankfurt.ogg}}) is a German professional [[sports club]] based in [[Frankfurt]], Hesse. It is best known for its [[football club]], which was founded on 8 March 1899. The club currently plays in the [[Bundesliga]], the top tier of the [[German football league system]]. Eintracht have won the [[List of German football champions|German championship]] once, the [[DFB-Pokal]] five times, the [[UEFA Europa League]] twice and finished as runner-up in the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] (now known as the Champions League) once. The team was one of the founding members of the Bundesliga at its inception<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kicker.de/die-gruendungsmitglieder-der-bundesliga-572341/slideshow|title=Die Gründungsmitglieder der Bundesliga|website=kicker|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> and has spent a total of 57 seasons in the top division, thus making them the seventh longest participating club in the highest tier of the league.

The club has 155,000 members, and thus is the fourth largest club playing in German football.<ref>"[https://klub.eintracht.de/news/strukturelle-einigkeit-25-jahre-eintracht-frankfurt-fussball-ag-169547/ Strukturelle Einigkeit]", weltfussball, 1 July 2025,</ref>

Since 1925 their stadium has been the [[Waldstadion (Frankfurt)|Waldstadion]], which is currently named Deutsche Bank Park for sponsorship reasons.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thestadiumbusiness.com/2020/04/01/commerzbank-arena-become-deutsche-bank-park/|title=Commerzbank-Arena To Become Deutsche Bank Park|date=1 April 2020|work=The Stadium Business|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref>

Eintracht Frankfurt have either won or drawn more than three-quarters of their games as well as having finished the majority of their seasons placed in the top half of the table,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bundesliga.com/de/bundesliga/clubs/eintracht-frankfurt/stats|title=Eintracht Frankfurt {{!}} Statistik|website=Bundesliga|access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref> but also having the highest number of losses in the league (717).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fussballdaten.de/bundesliga/ewige-tabelle/|title=Die ewige Tabelle der Bundesliga|website=Fussballdaten|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> With an average [[List of sports attendance figures|attendance]] of 59,071 in the 2025-26 Bundesliga season, the 4th highest attendance in the league.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/282985/clubs-of-german-football-bundesliga-by-average-attendance/?srsltid=AfmBOoo7-lUFs-d9mOiPsEszwv6HWhG4GkIy8hlMvVb2iuCJlwgL2g2T|title=Average match attendance in the Bundesliga in 2025/26, by club
|date=16 July 2026|website=statista.com|access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref> The player with the highest number of appearances (602) in the Bundesliga, [[Charly Körbel]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/players/duit-bundesliga-matches.html|title=Germany – All-Time Most Matches Played in Bundesliga|date=20 June 2019|publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> spent his entire senior career as a [[Defender (association football)|defender]] for Eintracht Frankfurt. The club's primary rival is local club [[Kickers Offenbach]], although, due to spending most of their history in different divisions, the two have only played two league matches within the last 40 years.{{when|date=January 2024|reason='within the last 40 years'? the source is from... 2009.}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fr.de/eintracht-frankfurt/eine-historische-fussball-feindschaft-11499950.html|title=Eine historische Fußball-Feindschaft |website=Frankfurter Rundschau |date=31 July 2009 |language=de |access-date=31 July 2009}}</ref>

With almost 14,000 active athletes in over 50 sports in 2024, Eintracht Frankfurt is the largest [[multi-sports club]] in the world with a professional football team.<ref name="Eintracht Frankfurt f441">{{cite web | title=Eintracht liegt weltweit auf Rang eins | website=Eintracht Frankfurt | url=https://klub.eintracht.de/news/eintracht-liegt-weltweit-auf-rang-eins-156617/ | language=de | access-date=11 February 2024}}</ref>

==History==
{{see also|List of Eintracht Frankfurt seasons}}

===Club origins===
[[File:Frankfurter FC Viktoria 1899.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The first team of Frankfurter Fußball-Club Victoria in 1899]]
The origins of the club go back to a pair of football clubs founded in 1899: ''Frankfurter Fußball-Club Victoria von 1899'' – regarded as the original team in the club's history – and ''Frankfurter Fußball-Club Kickers von 1899''.<ref name=DieAnfänge>{{cite web|url=https://museum.eintracht.de/chronik/1899-1920/|publisher=Eintracht Franakfurt|title=1899–1920 Die Anfänge des Fußballs in Frankfurt 1899–1920|language=de|access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref> Both clubs were founding members of the new [[Nordkreis-Liga]] in 1909.{{citation needed|date=January 2024}} These two teams merged in May 1911 to become ''Frankfurter Fußball Verein (Kickers-Victoria)'', an instant success, taking three league titles from 1912 to 1914 in the Nordkreis-Liga and qualifying for the Southern German championship in each of those seasons.<ref name=DieAnfänge /> In turn, ''Frankfurter FV'' joined the gymnastics club ''Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861'' to form ''TuS Eintracht Frankfurt von 1861'' in 1920.<ref name=fusion>{{cite web|url=https://museum.eintracht.de/chronik/1920-1933/|publisher=Eintracht Franakfurt|title=1920–1933 Fusion am Riederwald: Die Eintracht entsteht|language=de|access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref> The German word ''Eintracht'' means 'harmony' or 'concord', and so ''Eintracht'' is the equivalent of ''United'' in English in the names of sports teams.<ref>''Harper Collins German Dictionary: German-English/English-German'' (Harpercollins, 1991; {{ISBN|0061002437}}), p. 203.</ref>[[File:Spielszene_Karlsruher_FV_gegen_Eintracht_Frankfurt_in_der_Oberliga_Sued.jpg|thumb|right|260px|Oberliga Süd match in 1946: Karlsruher FV v Eintracht Frankfurt]]
At the time, sports in Germany was dominated by nationalistic gymnastics organizations, and under pressure from that sport's governing authority, the gymnasts and footballers went their separate ways again in 1927, as ''Turngemeinde Eintracht Frankfurt von 1861'' and ''Sportgemeinde Eintracht Frankfurt (FFV) von 1899''.<ref name=fusion />
[[File:Eintracht Frankfurt Performance Chart.png|300px|thumb|Historical chart of Eintracht Frankfurt league performance]]

Through the late 1920s and into the 1930s, Eintracht won a handful of local and regional championships, first in the [[Kreisliga Nordmain]], then in the [[Bezirksliga Main]] and [[Bezirksliga Main-Hessen]]. After being eliminated from the national level playoffs after quarterfinal losses in 1930 and 1931, they won their way to the final in 1932 where they were beaten 2–0 by [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]], who claimed their first ever German championship. In 1933, German football was re-organized into sixteen Gauligen under the [[Nazi Germany|Third Reich]], and the club played first division football in the [[Gauliga Südwest]], consistently finishing in the upper half of the table and winning their division in 1938.

Eintracht picked up where they left off after World War II, joining the new first division [[Oberliga Süd (1945-63)|Oberliga Süd]]. In 1946, Eintracht won the first [[Hessian Cup|Hessenpokal]], and finished third in the Oberliga Süd a year later. In 1953, they would win the Oberliga Süd title, qualifying Eintracht for the [[1953 German football championship|German championship]], though they did not make it to the final.

=== National champions and European Cup finalists ===
Former coach [[Paul Oßwald]] returned to the club for a third stint with Eintracht in 1958. In the [[1958–59 Oberliga|1958{{ndash}}59 season]] the club won their Oberliga again, qualifying for the [[1959 German football championship|1959 German championship]]. Winning all six of the games in the group phase, Eintracht made it to the final with a perfect record; there, they would meet rivals [[Kickers Offenbach]], the club that Oßwald joined from, and the runners up behind Eintracht in the Oberliga Süd. Frankfurt went on to win the final 5{{ndash}}3 after extra time, becoming German champions for the first and so far only time in front of 75,000 fans in Berlin's [[Olympiastadion (Berlin)|Olympiastadion]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thacker |first=Gary |date=28 March 2016 |title=Eintracht Frankfurt: the story of the other team in the greatest game ever played |url=https://thesefootballtimes.co/2016/03/28/frankfurt-the-story-of-the-other-team-in-the-greatest-game-ever-played/ |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=These Football Times |language=en-GB}}</ref>

As champions, Frankfurt would represent Germany in the [[1959–60 European Cup]], where they would come to international prominence. Having beaten [[BSC Young Boys]] and [[Wiener Sport-Club]] to make it to the semi-finals, they were drawn against Scottish champions [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]], who were considered favourites, at least in Scotland – Rangers manager [[Scot Symon]] allegedly asked, "Eintracht, who are they?" before the game.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McCracken |first=Craig |date=17 May 2022 |title=Rangers v Eintracht Frankfurt: a friendly rivalry forged in goals |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/beyond-the-last-man/2022/may/17/rangers-eintracht-frankfurt-friendly-rivalry-goals-europa-league-final |access-date=27 February 2023 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Eintracht won the first leg 6{{ndash}}1 at home, in a performance described as the greatest in the club's history.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Historie: Die Eintracht und die Glasgow Rangers |url=https://museum.eintracht.de/news/historie-die-eintracht-und-die-glasgow-rangers-141744 |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=Eintracht Frankfurt |language=de}}</ref> They would score six more in the second leg at [[Ibrox Stadium|Ibrox]], winning 12{{ndash}}4 on aggregate. After the game, the Rangers players gave their opponents a guard of honour as they left the pitch.

Eintracht would return to Glasgow for the [[1960 European Cup Final|final]] at [[Hampden Park]], although they lost 7–3 to [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]] despite taking an early lead. The final was widely regarded as one of the best football matches ever played, remembered for a [[List of UEFA Champions League hat-tricks|hat-trick]] by [[Alfredo Di Stéfano]] and four goals by [[Ferenc Puskás]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/blogs/philminshull/2010/05/the_great_european_cup_final_o.html|title=The great European Cup final of 1960 remembered|date=19 May 2010|publisher=BBC}}</ref>

After their championship-winning year, Eintracht did not win the Oberliga again, though they were runners-up in [[1960–61 Oberliga|1961]] and [[1961–62 Oberliga|1962]]. Both times they would finish second in the group phase of the German championship, missing out on the final.

===Founding member of the Bundesliga===
The side earned themselves a place as one of the original 16 teams selected to play in the [[Bundesliga]], Germany's new professional football league, formed in [[1963–64 Bundesliga|1963]].<ref name="Official">{{cite web|url= http://www.bundesliga.de/en/liga/news/2008/index.php?f=127776.php |title=The Bundesliga: a true success story| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110423074449/http://www.bundesliga.com/en/liga/news/2008/index.php?f=127776.php
 | archive-date=23 April 2011 |publisher=bundesliga.de |access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref> Eintracht played Bundesliga football for 33 consecutive seasons, finishing in the top half of the table for the majority of them. In the inaugural season, Eintracht finished 3rd behind [[1. FC Köln]] and [[MSV Duisburg|Meidericher SV]] – the club has still never managed a better Bundesliga finish – and also reached the [[1964 DFB-Pokal Final]].<ref>[https://www.dfb.de/maenner/wettbewerbe/dfb-pokal 1964 DFB-Pokal final – DFB]</ref>

Eintracht finished in the top half of the Bundesliga every season until [[1970–71 Bundesliga|1970–71]]. Although they didn't make it back to the European Cup, Eintracht did play in other non-UEFA European competitions, beating [[FK Inter Bratislava]] to win the [[1966–67 Intertoto Cup|1967 Intertoto Cup]] in the last season of its original format. That year, they also reached the semi-final of the [[1966–67 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup|Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]], losing to [[GNK Dinamo Zagreb|Dinamo Zagreb]].

===Cup successes===
[[File:Aankomst van het voetbalelftal van Eintracht Frankfurt op Schiphol i.v.m. de UEF, Bestanddeelnr 930-5808.jpg|thumb|[[Cha Bum-kun]], coach [[Friedel Rausch]], and [[Bernd Hölzenbein]] during Eintracht's successful [[1979–80 UEFA Cup]] campaign]]
From 1973 to 1981, Eintracht had arguably their most successful period of the Bundesliga era, winning three [[DFB-Pokal]]s and the [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cup]]. Many of the most iconic players from the club's history played during this era, such as [[Bernd Nickel]], [[Charly Körbel]], [[Bernd Hölzenbein]], [[Jürgen Grabowski]] and [[Cha Bum-kun]].

The first title success came under [[Dietrich Weise]] in the [[1973–74 DFB-Pokal]], winning 3{{ndash}}1 in the [[1974 DFB-Pokal Final|final]] over [[Hamburger SV]] – due to the [[1974 FIFA World Cup]], which Hölzenbein and Grabowski had won with [[Germany national football team|West Germany]], the final was not played until August 1974.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nicht über die Mittelinie |url=https://www.fr.de/eintracht-frankfurt/nicht-ueber-mittelinie-11062452.html |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=fr.de |date=23 May 2017 |language=de}}</ref>

Eintracht would win the cup again in 1975, beating [[MSV Duisburg]] 1{{ndash}}0. That season, they played in the [[UEFA Cup Winners' Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]] for the first time, and in the [[1975–76 European Cup Winners' Cup|1975–76]] campaign, they would go far, reaching the semi-finals. Despite beating [[West Ham United F.C.|West Ham]] 2–1 at home, Eintracht were beaten 3{{ndash}}1 in the second leg and were knocked out, while also finishing a relatively low ninth place in the Bundesliga. The club then had a difficult start to the [[1976–77 Bundesliga|1976–77]] season, but under new coach [[Gyula Lóránt]], appointed in November, Eintracht went unbeaten in the second half of the season. Lóránt, notable for introducing zonal marking to the Bundesliga,{{citation needed|date=January 2024}} took Frankfurt into fourth place by the end of the season, finishing only two points behind champions [[Borussia Mönchengladbach]]. Soon, however, Lóránt would leave for [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]], with [[Dettmar Cramer]] coming the other way to coach Frankfurt. Cramer left at the end of the disappointing [[1977–78 Bundesliga|1977–78]] season, replaced by [[Otto Knefler]], who soon had to leave on health grounds.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 June 2019 |title=Gyula Lorant: Der Mann, der die Raumdeckung nach Deutschland brachte |url=https://www.90min.de/posts/6394025-gyula-lorant-der-mann-der-die-raumdeckung-nach-deutschland-brachte |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=90min.de |language=de-DE |archive-date=28 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230228001440/https://www.90min.de/posts/6394025-gyula-lorant-der-mann-der-die-raumdeckung-nach-deutschland-brachte |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Fünf Trainer in einer Saison: Die Geschichte von Schalkes einzigem Vorgänger |url=https://www.kicker.de/fuenf-trainer-in-einer-saison-die-geschichte-von-schalkes-einzigem-vorgaenger-798610/artikel |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=kicker |language=de-DE}}</ref>

In January 1979, [[Friedel Rausch]] joined the club as head coach. This was one of two important arrivals in 1979, as [[Cha Bum-kun]] would sign for Eintracht in July, becoming the first Korean to play in Europe. He would quickly become an icon in Frankfurt, scoring 12 league goals in his debut season.<ref name="Pink">{{Cite web |last=Pink |date=19 October 2018 |title=Unlikely European Heroes, Part 3 – Eintracht Frankfurt |url=https://footballpink.net/2018-10-19-unlikely-european-heroes-part-3-eintracht-frankfurt/ |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=Football Pink |language=en-GB}}</ref> Eliminating [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]], [[CS Dinamo București|Dinamo București]], [[Feyenoord]] and [[FC Zbrojovka Brno]] in the earlier rounds of the [[1979–80 UEFA Cup|UEFA Cup]], Eintracht reached the semi-finals, at which point only West German teams remained. Drawn against Bayern Munich, they won 5–1 in extra time to earn a place in the final.

Eintracht lost 3–2 in the first leg of the [[1980 UEFA Cup final|final]] to Borussia Mönchengladbach, the reigning champions. The two away goals, scored by [[Harald Karger]] and Hölzenbein, would prove crucial. Two weeks later, they hosted the return leg. With the score still at 0–0, Friedel Rausch sent on teenager [[Fred Schaub]] with 13 minutes to play. Almost immediately, Schaub scored what proved to be only goal of the game, winning Eintracht the title on away goals.<ref name="Pink"/>

As [[Lothar Buchmann]] succeeded Rausch, Eintracht won their third DFB-Pokal in [[1980–81 DFB-Pokal|1981]]. This effectively marked the end of Eintracht's golden period, as they began their battle with relegation.

===Mid-80s struggles and 1988 DFB-Pokal===
In [[1983–84 Bundesliga|1984]], they defeated [[MSV Duisburg]] 6–1 on aggregate in the relegation playoff after finishing 16th; in [[1985–86 Bundesliga|1986]] and [[1986–87 Bundesliga|1987]], they would finish 15th.

After years as a bottom-half club in the Bundesliga, Eintracht had a successful [[1987–88 Bundesliga|1987–88]] season, finishing in the top half of the league for the first time since 1982. More importantly, they won the [[1987–88 DFB-Pokal]], with a 1–0 win over [[VfL Bochum]] in the [[1988 DFB-Pokal Final|1988 final]]. The goalscorer was Hungarian [[Lajos Détári]], who became a hero among the club's fans. Only two days after the final, Détári was sold to [[Olympiacos F.C.|Olympiacos]] for a large fee, helping to pay the club's debts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paprika-Mann mit viel Gefühl |url=https://www.fr.de/eintracht-frankfurt/paprika-mann-viel-gefuehl-11078650.html |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=fr.de |date=26 May 2017 |language=de}}</ref>

In [[1988–89 Bundesliga|1988–89]] Eintracht found themselves in the relegation fight again. [[Jörg Berger]] was appointed coach and led the side to safety with a 4–1 aggregate win over [[1. FC Saarbrücken]] in the relegation playoff.

=== Title challenges in the early 90s and first relegation ===
[[File:2018-09-17 Eintracht Frankfurt Golf Open Uli Stein-8875 (cropped).jpg|thumb|150px|[[Uli Stein]]]]

A year later, Berger had taken the club to 3rd place, and was recognised as the best coach in the league. Berger left in 1991 after a 4th-place finish, but the squad now included players considered among the Bundesliga's best, such as [[Uwe Bein]], [[Uli Stein]], [[Jørn Andersen]], [[Manfred Binz]], [[Tony Yeboah]] and [[Andreas Möller]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brügelmann |first=Matthias |title=Sport Bild – 55 Jahre Bundesliga: 1963–2018 |year=2018 |isbn=9783667113269 |pages=132–133 |publisher=Delius Klasing & Company KG |language=DE}}</ref>

[[Dragoslav Stepanović]] took over as coach when Berger left, and Eintracht would finish 3rd in both seasons he coached, although he left before the end of [[1992–93 Bundesliga|1992–93]]. Under Stepanović, Eintracht played what was considered some of the best football in Bundesliga history, making 'Stepi' a fan favourite to this day.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NACHRICHTEN |first=n-tv |title=Das "Lebbe" des Dragoslav Stepanovic |url=https://www.n-tv.de/leute/Das-Lebbe-des-Dragoslav-Stepanovic-article11218251.html |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=n-tv.de |language=de}}</ref> In [[1991–92 Bundesliga|1991–92]], the club came closer than ever before to winning the Bundesliga. Going into the last game of the season, Eintracht were top of the table and only needed a win against already-relegated [[FC Hansa Rostock|Hansa Rostock]]. With the scores level at 1–1 Eintracht were denied what seemed a clear penalty, they would go on to lose 2–1. Referee Alfons Berg later apologised for his decision, but [[VfB Stuttgart]] became champions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NACHRICHTEN |first=n-tv |title=Als Eintracht Frankfurt in Rostock eskalierte |url=https://www.n-tv.de/sport/fussball/redelings_nachspielzeit/Als-Eintracht-Frankfurt-in-Rostock-eskalierte-article19843045.html |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=n-tv.de |language=de}}</ref> Eintracht also came close in [[1993–94 Bundesliga|1993–94]], under [[Klaus Toppmöller]], leading the table at the halway point; however, they fell to 5th place and Toppmöller was sacked.

In the summer of 1994, [[Jupp Heynckes]] was appointed coach. Things quickly began to turn sour, as Heynckes fell out with key players Tony Yeboah, [[Maurizio Gaudino]] and [[Jay-Jay Okocha]]. The club suspended all three players; Yeboah and Gaudino soon left. With the club in 13th, Heynckes decided to leave. For his role in breaking up the successful side of the early 90s, Heynckes is still disliked by many fans in Frankfurt.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Als Jupp Heynckes Trainer von Eintracht Frankfurt war |url=https://www.fnp.de/eintracht-frankfurt/jupp-heynckes-trainer-eintracht-frankfurt-10440002.html |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=fnp.de |date=7 December 2017 |language=de}}</ref>

Relegation would come in [[1995–96 Bundesliga|1995–96]], with neither club legend Charly Körbel or the previously successful Dragoslav Stepanovic able to rescue Eintracht. After 33 consecutive years in the Bundesliga, Frankfurt went down alongside [[1. FC Kaiserslautern]], who had also been ever-present until 1996.

===Turbulent years===
After a tumultuous debut campaign in the [[2. Bundesliga]], Eintracht won the title in [[1997–98 2. Bundesliga|1997–98]] and returned to the Bundesliga. Promotion coach [[Horst Ehrmantraut]] left in December, and Jörg Berger returned to try to save Eintracht once more. On the final day of the [[1998–99 Bundesliga|1998–99]] season, Eintracht were expected to be relegated, but dramatically climbed out of the relegation zone on goal difference thanks to a late goal from [[Jan Åge Fjørtoft]] giving them a 5–1 win over Kaiserslautern.

The following year, in another struggle to avoid relegation, the club was docked two points for violating the conditions of their license.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Zwei Punkte Abzug für Eintracht Frankfurt {{!}} Bundesliga – kicker |url=https://www.kicker.de/zwei-punkte-abzug-fuer-eintracht-frankfurt-227507/artikel |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=[[Kicker (magazine)|Kicker]]}}</ref> Eintracht secured survival on the last day of the season with a win over [[SSV Ulm 1846|SSV Ulm]], who were relegated instead.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Heldt zitterte die Eintracht zum Klassenerhalt, Ulm steigt ab |url=https://www.kicker.de/frankfurt-gegen-ulm-2000-bundesliga-503339/analyse |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=kicker |language=de-DE}}</ref> Eintracht would go down{{vague|date=January 2024|reason='down'?}} the season afterwards with Friedel Rausch in charge, and did not come close to promotion in [[2001–02 2. Bundesliga|2001–02]].
[[File:Friedhelm Funkel bei Eintracht Frankfurt.JPG|thumb|[[Friedhelm Funkel]] as Eintracht Frankfurt coach]]
Eintracht secured a Bundesliga return on the final day of the [[2002–03 2. Bundesliga|2002–03]] season with a 6–3 win over [[SSV Reutlingen 05|Reutlingen]], dramatically scoring 3 in the last 10 minutes of the game.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Schur stürzt Mainz ins Tal der Tränen |url=https://www.kicker.de/frankfurt-gegen-ssv-reutlingen-2003-bundesliga-572763/analyse |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=kicker |language=de-DE}}</ref> They were then relegated straight back to the 2. Bundesliga, but were promoted again the season after, managed by [[Friedhelm Funkel]]. Funkel led the team to safety in [[2005–06 Bundesliga|2005–06]] and also took Eintracht to the [[2006 DFB-Pokal Final|DFB-Pokal final]] for the first time since 1988, where they lost to Bayern Munich. As Bayern had already qualified for Europe, this also meant that Eintracht qualified for the UEFA Cup. After years of stability under Funkel, [[Michael Skibbe]] replaced him in 2009.

The [[2010–11 Bundesliga|2010–11 season]] ended with the club's fourth Bundesliga relegation. After setting a new record for most points in the first half of the season, the club struggled after the winter break, going seven games without scoring a goal. Coach Skibbe was replaced with [[Christoph Daum]], but Eintracht were relegated again after winning just once in the second half of the season.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uefa.com/memberassociations/association=ger/news/newsid=1610804.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110323141024/http://www.uefa.com/memberassociations/association=ger/news/newsid=1610804.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=23 March 2011|title=Eintracht turn to Daum after Skibbe sacking|date=22 March 2011|publisher=UEFA}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uefa.com/memberassociations/association=ger/news/newsid=1630569.html|url-status=dead|title=Dortmund condemn Eintracht to the drop|date=14 May 2011|publisher=UEFA}}</ref>{{New archival link needed|date=April 2026}}

One year later, Eintracht defeated [[Alemannia Aachen]] 3–0 on the 32nd matchday of the [[2011–12 2. Bundesliga|2011–12 season]], securing promotion to the Bundesliga.<ref>[http://www.fr-online.de/eintracht-frankfurt/aufstieg-eintracht-frankfurt-ist-zurueck-in-der-1--liga,1473446,14979736.html FR-Online], Eintracht Frankfurt ist zurück in der 1. Liga. Retrieved 2 May 2012</ref> This was followed up by a 6th-place finish in the Bundesliga in [[2012–13 Bundesliga|2012–13]], qualifying Frankfurt for the [[UEFA Europa League|Europa League]].

===DFB Pokal and Europa League winners, participation in European competitions===
[[Image:FC Salzburg gegen SG Eintracht Frankfurt (28. Februar 2020 EL Sechzehntelfinale Rückspiel) 46.jpg|right|200px|thumb|Eintracht Frankfurt before the Europa League match at FC Salzburg on 28 February 2020]]
Having finished in the top half in [[2014–15 Bundesliga|2014–15]], a season in which Eintracht's [[Alexander Meier]] was the league's top scorer, the team struggled again in [[2015–16 Bundesliga|2015–16]] and [[Niko Kovač]] was appointed coach in March 2016. Frankfurt survived only through the relegation playoff; ending the season in 16th place, they beat 1. FC Nürnberg 2–1 on aggregate in the playoff. In Kovač's first full year, his team survived comfortably and also reached the [[2017 DFB-Pokal Final|final]] of the [[2016-17 DFB-Pokal|2017 DFB-Pokal]], where they were beaten by Borussia Dortmund.<ref>{{Cite web |title=From Berlin to Bayern: Niko Kovac gets his chance – DW – 04/13/2018 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/from-berlin-to-bayern-niko-kovac-gets-his-shot-at-the-big-time/a-43380990 |access-date=27 February 2023 |publisher=Deutsche Welle |language=en}}</ref>

Eintracht reached their second DFB-Pokal final in a row in [[2017–18 DFB-Pokal|2017–18]], this time winning 3–1 against heavy favourites Bayern Munich – who Kovač had already agreed to join from next season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bayern take consolation in Kovac as Frankfurt win German Cup – DW – 05/20/2018 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/bayern-munich-take-consolation-in-kovac-as-frankfurt-seal-german-cup-title/a-43857114 |access-date=27 February 2023 |publisher=Deutsche Welle |language=en}}</ref> He was replaced by [[Adi Hütter]].

In [[2018–19 Bundesliga|2018–19]], Eintracht's attacking trio of [[Luka Jović]], [[Ante Rebić]] and [[Sébastien Haller]] won lots of praise for their outstanding performances, scoring 41 league goals and 16 [[2018–19 UEFA Europa League|Europa League]] goals between them and earning the nickname "the Buffalo Herd".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trio Infernale, Büffelherde, Fußball 2000 reloaded: Der Angriff von Eintracht Frankfurt sorgt für Furore |url=https://www.bundesliga.com/de/bundesliga/news/eintracht-frankfurt-rebic-haller-jovic-fussball2000-trio-furore.jsp |access-date=27 February 2023 |website=bundesliga.de – die offizielle Webseite der Bundesliga |language=de}}</ref>  Making only their second appearance in the modern Europa League, Eintracht won all six group games against [[S.S. Lazio|Lazio]], [[Apollon Limassol FC|Apollon Limassol]] and [[Olympique de Marseille|Marseille]], and beat highly rated opponents [[FC Shakhtar Donetsk|Shakhtar Donetsk]], [[Inter Milan]] and [[S.L. Benfica|Benfica]]. In the semi-finals against [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]], Eintracht drew both legs 1–1 but ended up losing on penalties at [[Stamford Bridge (stadium)|Stamford Bridge]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/live/2019/may/09/chelsea-v-eintracht-frankfurt-europa-league-semi-final-second-leg-live?page=with:block-5cd497828f086f179813e8a2#liveblog-navigation|title=Chelsea 1–1 Eintracht Frankfurt (2–2 agg, 4–3 pens): Europa League semi-final – as it happened|work=The Guardian|date=9 May 2019}}</ref> Chelsea would go on to win the tournament. Eintracht also missed out on Champions League qualification in the Bundesliga, dropping from 4th to 7th after losing their last two games.

With Jović, Rebić and Haller all leaving in the summer of 2019, Eintracht regressed in [[2019–20 Bundesliga|2019–20]] and failed to qualify for Europe, but returned to the Europa League with a 5th-place finish in [[2020–21 Bundesliga|2020–21]], after which Adi Hütter left for Borussia Mönchengladbach. In the [[2021–22 UEFA Europa League|2021–22 Europa League]], Eintracht topped their group and stunned [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] in the quarter finals, taking a 3–0 lead at the [[Camp Nou]] and eventually winning 3–2 with approximately 30,000 travelling Frankfurt fans in attendance.<ref>{{Cite news |date=14 April 2022 |title=Frankfurt's Filip Kostic doubles up to dump Barcelona out of Europa League |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2022/apr/14/eintrachy-frankfurt-filip-kostic-doubles-up-to-dump-barcelona-out-of-europa-league |access-date=28 February 2023 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Steinberg |first1=Jacob |date=15 April 2022 |title=Barcelona 'ashamed' as almost 30,000 Frankfurt fans get into Camp Nou |language=en-GB |work=The Observer |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2022/apr/15/barcelona-ashamed-as-almost-30000-frankfurt-fans-get-into-camp-nou |access-date=28 February 2023 |agency=Reuters |issn=0029-7712}}</ref> Eintracht went on to beat West Ham home and away in the semi-finals to set up their first European final since 1980.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Terry |first=Dylan |date=5 May 2022 |title=Frankfurt vs West Ham LIVE: Europa League result, final score and reaction as Cresswell red card costs Hammers |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/west-ham-frankfurt-live-stream-score-result-2022-b2072376.html |access-date=7 May 2025 |work=The Independent |language=en}}</ref>

In the [[2022 UEFA Europa League final|final]] in Seville's [[Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium]], Frankfurt beat [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] 5–4 on penalties after a 1–1 draw in extra-time, with [[Rafael Santos Borré]] scoring Eintracht's goal and the winning penalty.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20220518-eintracht-frankfurt-beat-rangers-on-penalties-to-win-europa-league |title=Eintracht Frankfurt beat Rangers on penalties to win Europa League |website=France24 |date=19 May 2022 }}</ref> Goalkeeper [[Kevin Trapp]] was named [[Player of the match|man of the match]] in the final after making a crucial late save from [[Ryan Kent]] and saving [[Aaron Ramsey]]'s penalty in the shootout.<ref>{{Cite web |last=UEFA.com |date=18 May 2022 |title=Kevin Trapp named official UEFA Europa League final Hankook Player of the Match |url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/news/0275-152d4069c6c7-bb66addf55b4-1000--kevin-trapp-named-official-uefa-europa-league-final-hankook/ |access-date=28 February 2023 |publisher=UEFA |language=en}}</ref> Eintracht won the competition unbeaten; their success also qualified them for the [[2022–23 UEFA Champions League]], Eintracht's first appearance in the competition since 1960. Eintracht finished second in their Champions League group, qualifying for the knockout stages, but lost in the round of 16 against [[S.S.C. Napoli]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/64969965|title=Napoli 3–0 Eintracht Frankfurt|publisher=BBC|date=15 March 2023|accessdate=9 May 2023|first=Sam|last=Drury}}</ref> The team was more successful in the [[2022–23 DFB-Pokal]], reaching [[2023 DFB-Pokal final|the final]] on 3 June 2023, where they lost 2–0 against [[RB Leipzig]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Randal Kolo Muani seals Eintracht Frankfurt's DFB Cup final place with victory over VfB Stuttgart|url=https://www.bundesliga.com/en/bundesliga/news/stuttgart-eintracht-frankfurt-dfb-cup-live-team-news-match-stats-kolo-muani-gotze-23359|date=3 May 2023|accessdate=9 May 2023|publisher=Bundesliga}}</ref> A 7th-place finish at the end of [[2022–23 Bundesliga|2022–23]] season secured qualification for the [[UEFA Europa Conference League]].

Since November 2024, the executive board consists of Axel Hellmann (CEO), [[Markus Krösche]] (head of sports) and Julien Zamberk (head of finances) and Philipp Reschke (head of fan relations, merchandising and HR).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://klub.eintracht.de/fussball-ag/|title=Vorstand|date=28 January 2025|website=Eintracht Frankfurt|language=de|access-date=28 January 2025}}</ref>

==Colours, crest and nicknames==
[[File:DEU Frankfurt am Main COA.svg|thumb|right|125px|The Eintracht crest is based on the city coat of arms.]]The club crest derives from the coat of arms of the city of [[Frankfurt]], which itself is a reference to the one-headed [[Reichsadler|Imperial Eagle]] of the 13th century.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.holyromanempireassociation.com/heraldic-council-of-the-holy-roman-empire.html|title=The Heraldic Council of the Holy Roman Empire|website=Holy Roman Empire Association|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref>

The crest has evolved showing little significant change until 1980, when a stylized eagle in black and white was chosen to represent the team.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.eintracht-archiv.de/adler/adler.html|title=Wappen|website=Eintracht Archive|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> In Eintracht's centenary year of 1999, the club decided to re-adopt a more traditional eagle crest. Since 2005, Eintracht has had a living mascot, a [[golden eagle]] named ''Attila'' from the nearby [[Hanau]] Zoo,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.spiegel.de/sport/fussball/eintracht-adler-attila-gruesst-vom-videowuerfel-a-366941.html|title=Attila grüßt vom Videowürfel|date=26 July 2005|website=SPIEGEL Sport|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eintracht.de/en/squad/attila/|title=Attila|website=Eintracht Frankfurt|access-date=8 April 2020|archive-date=21 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160821080012/http://www.eintracht.de/en/squad/attila/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The official club colours of red, black, and white have their origins in the colours of the founding clubs ''Frankfurter FC Viktoria'' and ''Frankfurter FC Kickers'', which sported red and white and black and white respectively. Red and white are the colours of the city coat of arms, and black and white the colours of [[Coat of arms of Prussia|Prussia]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.eintracht-archiv.de/tachauch.html|title=Rot – Schwarz – Weiß|website=Eintracht Archiv|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref> When the clubs merged, officials decided to adopt the colours of both sides. Since local rival ''[[Kickers Offenbach]]'' sport the colours red and white, ''Eintracht'' avoids playing in such a kit, preferring to play in black and red, or in black and white. In the 2023–2024 season, the home kit is black and red.<ref name="Eintracht Frankfurt o549">{{cite web | title=Eintracht Frankfurt Heimtrikot für die Saison 2023/24 | website=Eintracht Frankfurt | url=https://stores.eintracht.de/fanshop/eintracht-frankfurt-heimtrikot-fuer-die-saison-2023-24/ | language=de | access-date=27 January 2024 | archive-date=27 January 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240127084748/https://stores.eintracht.de/fanshop/eintracht-frankfurt-heimtrikot-fuer-die-saison-2023-24/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>

In the [[2021–22 UEFA Europa League]], the Eagles played an unbeaten campaign, mostly sporting an all-white kit that gained them the nickname ''la bestia blanca'' (literally ''the white beast'' in Spanish), a wordplay on the Spanish term ''la bestia negra'' (literally ''the black beast'', also meaning ''bogey team'' in Spanish). This nickname was received after Eintracht knocked [[FC Barcelona]] out of the competition at [[Camp Nou]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/rangers/white-beasts-why-rangers-will-be-allowed-to-wear-usual-colours-against-eintracht-frankfurt-3696659|title='White beasts': Why Rangers will be allowed to wear usual colours against Eintracht Frankfurt|website=The Scotsman|access-date=17 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://profis.eintracht.de/news/rueckkehr-zur-normalitaet-und-die-geburtsstunde-der-bestia-blanca-146861|title=Rückkehr zur Normalität und die Geburtsstunde der Bestia Blanca|website=Eintracht.de|access-date=15 December 2022}}</ref>
[[File:Eintracht Frankfurt historial.png|right|450px|thumb|Eintracht's eagle (''Adler'') over the years: the logo of ''Frankfurter FV'' 1911 and the red eagle of ''TuS Eintracht Frankfurt'' 1920 and ''Sportgemeinde Eintracht Frankfurt'' 1967 before today's more traditional style logo was adopted]]

The club is nicknamed "''Die Adler''" ("The Eagles"), which derives from their logo. A nickname still popular among supporters is ''SGE'', taken from the club's old official name '''''S'''port'''g'''emeinde '''E'''intracht'' (Frankfurt), which roughly translates into English as "Sports Community Harmony."

The nickname ''Launische Diva'' ("Moody Diva") was heard most often in the early 1990s, when the club would comfortably defeat top teams only to surprisingly lose to lesser clubs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://de.fifa.com/news/die-launische-diva-vom-main-1628125|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190404200106/https://de.fifa.com/news/die-launische-diva-vom-main-1628125|url-status=dead|archive-date=4 April 2019|title=Die launische Diva vom Main|date=9 May 2012|publisher=FIFA|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.spiegel.de/video/wie-eintracht-zum-namen-launische-diva-kam-video-1229760.html|title=Wie die Eintracht zur launischen Diva wurde|date=17 February 2013|website=SPIEGEL Sport|access-date=8 April 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.extratipp.com/eintracht-frankfurt/eintracht-frankfurt-launische-diva-geschichte-11811587.html|title=Die 'launische Diva' ist Geschichte|date=28 February 2019|website=Extra Tipp|access-date=8 April 2020|archive-date=20 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420215147/https://www.extratipp.com/eintracht-frankfurt/eintracht-frankfurt-launische-diva-geschichte-11811587.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The nickname ''Schlappekicker'' ("Slipper Kickers") has been around since the 1920s, when ''J. & C. A. Schneider'', a local manufacturer of shoes and especially slippers (called ''Schlappe'' in the regional [[Hessian dialects|Hessian dialect]]) was a major financial backer of the club and helped propel it to national relevance.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fr.de/politik/judebuwwe-11727888.html|title=STIMMT DAS? "Judebuwwe"|date=9 May 2005|work=Frankfurter Rundschau|access-date=30 January 2021}}</ref>

==Stadium==
{{Main|Waldstadion (Frankfurt)}}
[[File:Deutsche bank park.jpg|thumb|250px|[[Waldstadion (Frankfurt)|Deutsche Bank Park]]]]

The club's initial games from 1899 to 1906 were played on the former ''Hundswiese'' field, whose present day location would be near [[Hessischer Rundfunk]]. Following new regulations that pitches needed to be surrounded by a fence for the purpose of official games, the team established a new pitch by the [[Eschersheim|Eschersheimer Landstraße]] called ''Victoriaplatz'' in 1906, for which they purchased stands at a price of 350 [[German gold mark|marks]] in 1908. From 1912 the team moved to a new ground at Roseggerstraße in [[Dornbusch (Frankfurt am Main)|Dornbusch]] with more facilities, before relocating to the former [[Riederwaldstadion]] in 1920 following the fusion of ''Frankfurter FV'' and ''Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861.''

The ground was inaugurated as Waldstadion ("Forest Stadium") in 1925 with the German championship final match between [[FSV Frankfurt]] vs. [[1. FC Nürnberg]].
<!--more information needed here-->
The facility was renovated for the FIFA World Cup 2006 in Germany. {{as of|2026}}, for Bundesliga fixtures the maximum capacity is 60,100.<ref name="Stadionwelt 1970 g983">{{cite web | title=Neue Nordwestkurve im Deutsche Bank Park eingeweiht | website=Stadionwelt | date=1 January 1970 | url=https://www.stadionwelt.de/news/69542/neue-nordwestkurve-im-deutsche-bank-park-eingeweiht | language=de | access-date=28 December 2023}}</ref>

Though the media usually refer to the ground by the official name, Deutsche Bank Park, Eintracht fans faithful typically use the original name, Waldstadion.

==Reserve team==
{{Main|Eintracht Frankfurt II}}
Eintracht Frankfurt U21 is the reserve team of Eintracht Frankfurt. The team played as U23 (Under 23) to emphasize the character of the team as a link between the youth academy and professional team. The club board decided to dissolve the team after the 2013–14 season while playing in the regular league system in the fourth tier, the [[Regionalliga Süd (1994–2012)|Regionalliga Süd]]. 
On 14 February 2022, Eintracht Frankfurt applied to have a reserves team to be re-admitted to the [[German football league system#Hesse|5th tier]] [[Hessenliga]] for the 2022–23 season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://en.eintracht.de/news/antrag-auf-neuaufnahme-einer-zweiten-mannschaft-139300|title=Application for new reserve team|language=en|website=eintracht.de|date=14 February 2022|access-date=14 February 2022}}</ref>
In the first season after being re-admitted, Frankfurt II won the Hessenliga and got promoted to the [[Regionalliga Südwest]], where they play now.

==Rivalries and friendships==
[[File:Match Frankfurt - Marseille in November 2018.jpg|thumb|Eintracht Frankfurt supporters performance]]

The club's main rival is from across the [[Main (river)|Main]] river, the side [[Kickers Offenbach]]. The clubs played the [[1959 German football championship Final|1959 German championship final]], which Eintracht won.<ref name="Hettfleisch">{{cite web |first=Wolfgang |last=Hettfleisch | title=Eine historische Fußball-Feindschaft | publisher=[[Frankfurter Rundschau]] | date=26 January 2019 | url=https://www.fr.de/eintracht-frankfurt/eine-historische-fussball-feindschaft-11499950.html | language=de | access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref>

Eintracht also maintain rivalries with [[SV Darmstadt 98|Darmstadt 98]] regionally, known as the ''[[Hesse]] derby'', as well with [[1. FSV Mainz 05]] and [[1. FC Kaiserslautern]] in Rhineland-Palatinate.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.spiegel.de/sport/fussball/bundesliga-eintracht-frankfurt-fans-duerfen-darmstadt-nicht-betreten-a-1089414.html|title=Hessenderby: Darmstädter Polizei errichtet Sperrzone für Eintracht-Fans|website=Der Spiegel|date=26 April 2016 }}</ref>

The club's original rival was [[Frankfurt]] city-rival [[FSV Frankfurt]]. In both clubs' early years, there was a fierce rivalry, but after World War II Eintracht proved to be the stronger and the rivalry deteriorated due to lack of contact.<ref name="Reich" /> {{Asof|2024}}, the fan relations tend to be friendly.<ref name="Reich">{{cite web | last=Reich | first=Stephan | title=FSV und Eintracht Frankfurt: Erst Feind, dann Freund | website=hessenschau.de | date=12 October 2024 | url=https://www.hessenschau.de/sport/fussball/regionalliga/fsv-und-eintracht-frankfurt-erst-feind-dann-freund-v1,fsv-sge-history-100.html | language=de | access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> 
The [[2011–12 2. Bundesliga|2011–12 season]] saw Eintracht play FSV in a league match for the first time in almost 50 years. The last league game between the two had been played on 27 January 1962, then in the [[Oberliga Süd (1945–63)|Oberliga Süd]]. For the first of the two matches, FSV's home game on 21 August 2011, the decision was made to move to Eintracht's stadium as FSV's [[Stadion am Bornheimer Hang|Bornheimer Hang]] holds fewer than 11,000 spectators.<ref>[https://www.kicker.de/st-pauli-schiesst-sich-spaet-in-den-hoehenrausch-556647/artikel Das Frankfurter Derby elektrisiert] {{in lang|de}} www.kicker.de, published: 21 August 2011. Retrieved 21 August 2011</ref> Eintracht won 4–0.<ref name="v550">{{cite | title=Köhler schlägt doppelt zu | url=https://www.kicker.de/fsv-frankfurt-gegen-frankfurt-2011-bundesliga-1143031/analyse | language=de-DE | access-date=11 September 2026 | page=}}</ref> The second match on 18 February 2012 ended in another victory for Eintracht, a 6–1 rout.<ref name="a014">{{cite web | title=Spielinfo | website=kicker | url=https://www.kicker.de/frankfurt-gegen-fsv-frankfurt-2012-bundesliga-1143184/spielinfo | language=de-DE | access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref>

A friendship between two Eintracht fan clubs and supporters of English club [[Oldham Athletic A.F.C.|Oldham Athletic]] has lasted for over 30 years after fans from each club met at an international football tournament.<ref name="Shaw">{{cite web | last=Shaw | first=David | title=Adler und Eulen: zwei Vereine, eine Freundschaft | publisher=VICE | date=7 August 2015 | url=https://www.vice.com/de/article/adler-und-eulen-zwei-vereine-eine-freundschaft-271/ | access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> Eintracht supporters also have an international friendship with supporters of Italian club [[Atalanta BC|Atalanta]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2014/jan/07/atalanta-serie-a-club-guide-ground-ultras-caniggia|title=Atalanta: Serie A alternative club guide |first=Richard |last=Hall |date=7 January 2014 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/who-german-football-hooligans-linked-13941978 |title=Who are the German 'football hooligans' linked with Concert Square carnage? |last=Prentice |first=David |date=23 November 2017 |work=[[Liverpool Echo]] |accessdate=10 August 2021}}</ref>
